claims.text: The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a homogeneous alloy structure.
Aberration-corrected TEM can be used to observe the nanoparticles during in situ high-temperature heating.
A TEM heating holder can provide controlled high-temperature conditions while the AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are imaged.
Atomic-resolution TEM imaging can be maintained from approximately 500 °C to 900 °C.
Heating will produce atomic rearrangements in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Heating may cause local phase segregation in AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
Heating may alter grain boundaries in ways that act as stabilizing features.
Thermal energy increases atomic mobility within the nanoparticles.
Thermally driven atomic rearrangements minimize the nanoparticles' free energy.
The rearrangements can form more stable interfaces or defect configurations.
More stable interfaces or defect configurations enhance overall thermal stability relative to the as-synthesized state.
Real-time imaging will reveal temperature-dependent reordering or phase adjustments.
The observed structural changes will correlate with a thermal-stabilization mechanism.
Current theoretical models predict enhanced thermal stability from thermodynamic contributions.
Direct atomic-scale experimental validation of the proposed rearrangements is currently lacking.
Electron-beam effects can cause the observed behavior to differ from intrinsic thermal behavior.

Failure to observe significant rearrangements, phase transitions, or defect-mediated stabilization across the specified temperature range would falsify the proposed rearrangement-based stabilization hypothesis.
